# Abstract

The eastern half of Timor Island, encompassing the contemporary territory of Timor-Leste alongside the historic enclave of Oecusse-Ambeno and Atauro Island (16.917 km² across 233 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells), formed an isolated maritime periphery of the Portuguese seaborne empire for more than four centuries. From the initial arrival of Portuguese navigators and Dominican friars off Lifau in 1515 to the abrupt termination of colonial rule in November 1975, the demographic evolution of the territory was shaped by a continuous tension between rugged interior mountain topography and coastal colonial enclaves. Indigenous Timorese communities maintained lineage-based socio-political structures centred on sacred houses (*uma lulik*) and territorial chiefdoms (*rai*), resisting direct administrative subjugation through extensive upland settlement networks, shifting swidden cultivation and strategic alliances with Topasse Eurasian lineages.

Reconstructed across three administrative sub-regions from 1515 to 1975 under MANDALA, aggregate population expanded from 160k inhabitants in 1515 during initial European contact to 210k in 1700 and 280k in 1800. Population growth accelerated during the nineteenth century as coffee cultivation expanded across Ermera, Liquica and Ainaro, reaching 340k in 1860 and 380k in 1900. Following the suppression of the Great Rebellion of Manufahi in 1912 and the imposition of head taxes, population rose to 451k in 1927 and 463k in 1936. During the Pacific War (1942 to 1945), brutal Japanese military occupation, Allied aerial bombing and guerrilla warfare triggered severe demographic contraction, with population receding to 420k in 1946 (representing a catastrophic loss of over 43k lives through excess mortality, famine and displaced birth cohorts). Post-war recovery under colonial development plans restored demographic momentum, lifting total population to 442k in 1950, 517k in 1960, 609k in 1970 and 660k in 1975 (yielding an aggregate density of 3.901,4 persons per 100 km², or 39,01 persons per km²).

Demographic mass remained distributed across three contrasting ecological and administrative zones. At the 1975 apex, the Western Districts and Oecusse-Ambeno Enclave accommodated 257,4k people (39% of regional population; 4.228,68 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the fertile coffee uplands of Ermera, Hatulia and Ainaro alongside the coastal redoubt of Pante Makassar. The Eastern Districts (encompassing Baucau, Lautem, Viqueque and Manufahi) housed 224,4k inhabitants (34%; 3.940,99 persons per 100 km²), supported by extensive rice plains in Viqueque, limestone plateaux in Lautem and the Baucau market basin. The Dili, Liquica and Central North Coast division accommodated 178,2k people (27%; 3.469,63 persons per 100 km²), dominated by the colonial administrative capital of Dili, the maritime shipping port of Liquica and the arid coastal scrub lowlands of Manatuto.

This historical demographic synthesis reconciles 154 catalogued settlement trajectories with four centuries of Portuguese administrative reports, Dominican mission registries, official twentieth-century censuses and geomorphological habitat modelling. By subtracting nucleated coastal settlements and administrative posts from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, the reconstruction isolates genuine agrarian population distributions from colonial fiscal exaggerations, providing an analytical foundation for eastern Indonesian historical demography.

# Background

## Environmental Gradients and Island Biogeography

The territory of Portuguese Timor is defined by steep topographical gradients, dynamic tectonic uplift and pronounced climatic variability [@Anonymous2022Democratic]. The island is traversed by a rugged central mountain spine (the Ramelau cordillera), which reaches an elevation of 2.963 m at Mount Tatamailau. This alpine divide separates the northern coastal plain from the southern littoral, creating two distinct hydroclimatic regimes [@Anonymous2022Democratic].

The northern coast experiences an extended dry season lasting up to eight months, receiving less than 1.000 mm of annual rainfall. Here, short, steep river valleys discharge ephemeral torrents (*mota*) into the Ombai and Wetar straits, leaving riverbeds completely dry during the dry season and severely restricting lowland irrigated agriculture [@Anonymous2022Democratic]. In contrast, the southern slopes receive orographic moisture from both the northwest monsoon and the southeast trade winds, experiencing annual precipitation exceeding 2.000 mm and supporting denser moist deciduous and evergreen forests [@Almeida2024Symbology].

These environmental contrasts dictated indigenous settlement strategies. Throughout the pre-colonial and early modern eras, sedentary agricultural populations avoided the malarial coastal lowlands, establishing fortified villages (*koba*) along steep ridge bluffs between 600 m and 1.500 m elevation [@Clamagirand1972Travail]. In these mid-elevation zones, communities practised complex multi-cropping rotations based on drought-tolerant tubers (taro, yams), foxtail millet, rice, bananas and, from the seventeenth century onward, introduced American maize (*Zea mays*) [@Almeida2024Symbology; @Clamagirand1972Travail]. Highland forest borders provided grazing for indigenous Timorese water buffalo (*karau*) and mountain ponies, while native sandalwood groves (*Santalum album*) formed the primary commercial export asset [@Villiers1994Vanishing].

## Indigenous Social Formations and Customary Governance

Prior to European administrative penetration, eastern Timor was divided into dozens of autonomous and confederated petty kingdoms (*rai*), each ruled by a hereditary sovereign (*liurai*) supported by executive ministers (*dato*) and sacred councillors [@MeitznerYode2025Indigenous; @Kammen2017Metaphors]. Indigenous society was organised around sacred lineages (*uma lulik*), which controlled communal ancestral lands and mediated spiritual relations with territorial tutelary spirits (*rai na'in*) [@MeitznerYode2025Indigenous].

The socio-political fabric was bifurcated into distinct ethnolinguistic groupings:
1. Austronesian language speakers, including the Tetum, Mambai, Tokodede and Kemak, who occupied the central valleys, northern coffee ranges and southern river corridors [@Smith2002Timor; @Roben2026Formas].
2. Non-Austronesian (Papuan or Trans-New Guinea) language speakers, including the Fataluku, Makasae, Makalero and Bunak, concentrated in the eastern limestone plateaux of Lautem and Baucau alongside western mountainous borders [@Smith2002Timor].

Political cohesion across these diverse linguistic groups was maintained through ritual alliances (*fetosan-umane* marital exchange networks) and reciprocal blood-oath pacts (*hemu raan*) [@ROQUE2012Marriage]. Authority was dual: spiritual authority resided in the sacred lord of the land (*lulik*), who remained secluded in the ancestral house, while executive power was wielded by the war chief (*luraic* or *liurai*), who managed military defence, external trade and tributary collections [@MeitznerYode2025Indigenous; @Kammen2017Metaphors]. This decentralised political architecture proved remarkably resilient against external subjugation, allowing local rulers to absorb European military incursions and manipulate colonial alliances to enhance domestic status.

## Early Colonial Encounters and the Sandalwood Frontier (1515 to 1769)

Portuguese engagement with Timor began shortly after the capture of Malacca in 1511, driven by the lucrative international market for aromatic white sandalwood [@Villiers1994Vanishing; @Thomaz2020Cardoso]. Navigators first landed on the northern coast near Lifau (in contemporary Oecusse) around 1515, initiating seasonal trading visits [@PereiradosSa2026History]. By the late sixteenth century, Dominican friars established permanent Catholic mission stations on the adjacent island of Solor and at Lifau, baptising local chieftains and constructing fortified coastal trading stations [@PereiradosSa2026History; @Hagerdal2022Chapter].

During the seventeenth century, a distinct Eurasian community known as the Topasses (or *Larantuqueiros*, commonly termed "Black Portuguese") emerged from intermarriages between Portuguese traders, soldiers, sailors and local Timorese or Florinese women [@Hagerdal2022Chapter; @ROQUE2012Marriage]. Organised under the rival Hornay and Da Costa dynasties, the Topasses established a powerful commercial monopoly over interior sandalwood harvesting [@Villiers1994Vanishing]. Armed with European firearms and speaking a distinctive Portuguese-influenced contact language, the Topasses functioned as autonomous warlords, acknowledging Portuguese crown sovereignty only when it served their commercial interests [@Hagerdal2022Chapter].

When the Portuguese crown attempted to impose formal administrative control by dispatching Antonio Coelho Guerreiro as the first official governor to Lifau in 1702, Topasse leaders resisted fiercely [@PereiradosSa2026History]. The crown redoubt at Lifau was repeatedly besieged by Topasse armies and hostile Timorese confederations. Following decades of military skirmishes and devastating blockades, Governor Antonio Jose Telles de Meneses abandoned Lifau in 1769, relocating the colonial administration, military garrison and allied civilian population eastward to Dili, which became the permanent capital of Portuguese Timor [@PereiradosSa2026History; @Tosun2025Influence].

## Colonial Consolidation, Pacification Wars and Coffee Expansion (1769 to 1912)

The transfer of the colonial capital to Dili in 1769 coincided with the decline of the wild sandalwood trade due to widespread deforestation in accessible coastal valleys [@Villiers1994Vanishing]. To replace lost timber revenues, the colonial administration encouraged commercial plantation agriculture, introducing Arabica coffee (*Coffea arabica*) to the volcanic upland soils of Ermera, Liquica and Ainaro in the early nineteenth century [@Kammen2025Colonial; @Almeida2025Baldios].

Colonial authority throughout the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries remained largely illusory outside the immediate perimeter of Dili and coastal forts [@Roque2016Unruly]. Most interior *liurais* governed autonomously, receiving Portuguese military titles (such as *coronel* or *brigadeiro*) and ceremonial gifts in exchange for nominal fealty [@MeitznerYode2025Indigenous]. However, facing acute fiscal deficits and mounting pressure from the Netherlands (which consolidated control over western Timor), Governor Afonso de Castro instituted comprehensive administrative reforms in the 1860s, dividing the colony into ten military commands (*comandos militares*) and imposing a direct head tax (*finta*) on indigenous households [@Roque2016Unruly; @Goy1999Lindpendance].

The transition to direct administrative extraction provoked widespread anti-colonial rebellions:
1. The Moris and Covalima uprisings during the late nineteenth century, sparked by forced road labour (*corveia*) and military conscription [@Roque2016Unruly].
2. The Great Rebellion of Manufahi (1895 to 1912), led by Dom Boaventura, the *liurai* of Manufahi. Boaventura unified indigenous kingdoms across the central highlands and southern plains in an armed struggle against colonial taxes and land alienation [@Bovensiepen2019Pacificati; @Bovensiepen2022Chapter].

The rebellion was crushed only after protracted military campaigns commanded by Governor Jose Celestino da Silva and Governor Filomeno da Camara, who deployed metropolitan troops, gunboats and thousands of auxiliary indigenous warriors (*moradores*) from loyal kingdoms [@Bovensiepen2019Pacificati; @Sousa2023Insurrect]. The defeat of Dom Boaventura in 1912 marked the definitive military pacification of eastern Timor [@Roque2016Unruly]. The colonial regime dismantled the sovereignty of the *liurais*, subdividing traditional kingdoms into administrative *sucos* governed by colonial-appointed headmen and establishing civil administrative posts (*postos administrativos*) throughout the interior [@Sousa2023Chapter].

## Twentieth-Century Demography, Wartime Devastation and Modernisation (1912 to 1975)

Following the pacification campaigns, the colonial regime established civil administration (*administracao civil*), introducing modern census counts and intensifying the poll tax (*imposto de capitacao*), which forced rural men into seasonal wage labour on coffee plantations and public road construction [@Sousa2023Chapter; @Kammen2025Colonial]. Between 1912 and 1936, the territory experienced steady demographic expansion, with population rising from approximately 390k to 463k [@Saikia2011Investigation]. Catholic mission schools and rudimentary sanitary posts expanded into district centres such as Baucau, Ermera, Ainaro and Maliana, though health conditions remained precarious due to endemic malaria, tuberculosis and malnutrition [@Machado2025Rapidly].

This gradual growth was violently disrupted by the outbreak of the Pacific War in December 1941. Despite Portugal's formal neutrality, Allied forces (consisting of the Australian 2/2nd Independent Company and Dutch troops, known as Sparrow Force) occupied Portuguese Timor in December 1941 to prevent a Japanese advance toward Darwin [@Fernandes2022Australias]. In February 1942, the Imperial Japanese Army invaded the island with the 48th Division, initiating a brutal three-year guerrilla war [@Duek2025Introduction; @Fernandes2022Australias].

The Japanese military occupation caused severe devastation:
- Indigenous populations were forced to supply food rations and labour battalions (*heiho*) to Japanese garrisons, triggering catastrophic crop failures and widespread famine across the central highlands [@Duek2025Introduction].
- Allied air forces repeatedly bombed Dili, Baucau and coastal villages to destroy Japanese installations, levelling urban infrastructure [@Rocha2020Tempos].
- Inter-tribal warfare was weaponised by occupying forces; the Japanese armed the "Black Columns" (anti-Portuguese Timorese and Topasse irregulars) to hunt down Allied commandos and terrorise pro-Allied villages [@Duek2025Introduction; @Rocha2020Tempos].

Between 1942 and 1945, excess mortality, direct military massacres, forced displacement and famine claimed an estimated 40k to 60k Timorese lives [@Duek2025Introduction]. Total population dropped from 463k in 1936 to 420k in 1946, reflecting an acute wartime demographic contraction.

In the post-war era, the Portuguese government initiated comprehensive reconstruction programmes funded by metropolitan development plans (*Planos de Fomento*) [@Madeira2010Manipulation; @Kammen2018Progress]. Dili was completely rebuilt along a modern administrative plan, featuring broad avenues, port facilities and public schools [@Philpott2007Another]. Systematic vaccination campaigns against smallpox and yaws alongside DDT indoor residual spraying curtailed epidemic mortality, enabling rapid demographic recovery [@Saikia2011Investigation; @Silva2017Representations]. Population expanded from 442k in 1950 to 517k in 1960, 609k in 1970 and 660k in 1975, when the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon initiated an abrupt and tumultuous decolonisation process [@Nuttall2021Portuguese; @Kubiak2021East; @Feij2022Autodeterminao; @Pereira2024Singularities].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model historical demographic distribution across 16.917 km² of rugged island terrain, the MANDALA spatial engine partitions Portuguese Timor into 233 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Topographic slope and ruggedness: severe slope penalties are applied to vertical cliff escarpments in the Ramelau range, while moderate penalties are applied to mid-elevation highland basins (600 m to 1.200 m) that historically supported intensive garden swidden and coffee agroforestry [@Anonymous2022Democratic].
- Drainage proximity: cells within 5 km of perennial river confluences or springs receive positive weighting for domestic water access, while active mangrove estuaries subject to tidal saline inundation receive negative weighting [@Anonymous2022Democratic].
- Rainfall and agroclimatic zones: incorporating distinct precipitation masks that distinguish the drought-prone northern coast from the wetter southern river floodplains and eastern karst plateaux [@Almeida2024Symbology; @Clamagirand1972Travail].

Where regional archaeological substrata inform historical settlement priors across maritime and mainland Southeast Asia, baselines are calibrated against statutory heritage registries (including the Thailand Fine Arts Department FADGIS, Indonesia Kemendikbud Cagar Budaya, the Harvard Published Excavations Atlas, the Myanmar Bagan Inventory and the Dutch Oudheidkundige Dienst OV via NUSARC) rather than crowdsourced repositories.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated administrative settlements and dispersed agricultural cultivators, 154 catalogued settlements with longitudinal population series are anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across internal district borders, preventing step discontinuities between adjacent mountain valleys.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit uncertainty interval reflecting source documentation fidelity:
- Pre-colonial and early contact eras (1515 to 1700): +/- 14% to +/- 18%, accommodating reliance on early merchant travelogues, mission reports and carrying-capacity modelling.
- Nineteenth-century colonial era (1800 to 1860): +/- 10% to +/- 12%, calibrated against Governor Castro's tax rolls and military command estimates.
- Administrative census era (1900 to 1936): +/- 7% to +/- 9%, reflecting official civil registers and poll tax returns.
- Wartime benchmark (1946): +/- 9,5%, incorporating post-war damage assessments and displaced population surveys.
- Modern census era (1950 to 1975): +/- 2,5% to +/- 3%, based on the 1950, 1960 and 1970 official provincial censuses.

# Testing and Validation

## Archival Documentation and Census Synthesis

To construct reliable demographic baselines, this study synthesises four primary classes of historical documentation [@PereiradosSa2026History; @Roque2016Unruly]:
1. Early modern Portuguese chronicles and mission reports: archival records of the Dominican missions from Solor and Lifau, including seventeenth-century baptismal registers (*assentos de baptismo*) and correspondence preserved in the *Arquivo Historico Ultramarino* in Lisbon [@PereiradosSa2026History; @Hagerdal2022Chapter; @Matos2020Studies].
2. Nineteenth-century fiscal and military gazetteers: reports by Governors Afonso de Castro (1859 to 1865) and Jose Celestino da Silva (1894 to 1908), which recorded village household counts, tribute obligations (*finta*) and warrior recruitment quotas [@Roque2016Unruly; @Sousa2023Insurrect; @Kammen2025Colonial].
3. Mid-twentieth-century provincial censuses: the *Censo da Populacao da Provincia de Timor* conducted in 1950, 1960 and 1970, which recorded de jure and de facto populations down to the *posto administrativo* and *suco* level, disaggregated by civil status, age cohort and ethnic origin [@Madeira2010Manipulation; @Saikia2011Investigation].
4. Post-war reconstruction surveys: damage assessments compiled in 1946 and 1947 by the *Direccao dos Servicos de Administracao Civil*, detailing war mortality, famine displacement and livestock losses across all administrative districts [@Duek2025Introduction; @Rocha2020Tempos].

## Multi-Criteria Evaluation and Toponymic Concordance

Toponymic continuity presents major challenges in Timorese historical demography, as settlement names shifted between Portuguese colonial designations, indigenous Tetum forms and local dialect variants [@Smith2002Timor; @Roben2026Formas]. We deployed an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) framework to evaluate multi-criteria geographical and historical concordances [@MeitznerYode2025Indigenous; @Leach2015Politics]. Every catalogued settlement was georeferenced against modern topographic maps (1:50.000 Portuguese military cartography and modern satellite imagery), verifying that historical military command posts, administrative seats and church parishes align with contemporary *sucos*.

Where multiple colonial survey points fell within a 2,2 km spatial radius of a primary administrative centre, subordinate suburbs and military redoubts (such as Fort Santo Antonio of Lifau or Fort Nossa Senhora da Conceicao in Dili) were consolidated into the primary settlement record, preserving spatial independence and eliminating double counting [@PereiradosSa2026History; @Tosun2025Influence].

## Epidemiological Dynamics and Agricultural Calibrations

Historical population trajectories were cross-checked against epidemiological and subsistence models [@Clamagirand1972Travail; @Machado2025Rapidly]. Endemic malaria (*Plasmodium falciparum* and *Plasmodium vivax*) along the coastal littoral acted as a powerful demographic brake, depressing crude birth rates and elevating infant mortality prior to twentieth-century DDT campaigns. In the highlands, swidden productivity constrained maximum village sizes, explaining why rural Timorese populations remained dispersed across small lineage hamlets rather than concentrating in nucleated towns [@Clamagirand1972Travail].

The catastrophic demographic deficit between 1936 and 1946 was calibrated against caloric intake models during the Japanese occupation. The requisition of up to 70% of local grain harvests by occupation forces, combined with the destruction of seed stocks and forced corvee labour on coastal airfields, triggered widespread famine across Ermera, Bobonaro, Ainaro and Viqueque, validating the documented loss of over 43k lives [@Duek2025Introduction; @Rocha2020Tempos; @Fernandes2022Australias].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger for Portuguese Timor was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national census registries and subnational administrative tables, incorporating 95 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of historical administrative posts and church missions from colonial monographs and archival gazetteers, adding 42 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation audits, adding 17 early contact ports and interior market settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunter and homonym audits across all three sub-regions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 159 candidate localities were audited: 154 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 5 were excluded as duplicate homonyms or subordinate fortifications merged within 2,2 km.

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of Portuguese Timor across four and a half centuries demonstrates a protracted trajectory of low early modern growth, nineteenth-century acceleration, wartime crisis and rapid post-war recovery (Figure \ref{fig:demography} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Five Historical Demographic Epochs

### Early Contact and the Sandalwood Extraction Era (1515 to 1700)

During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Portuguese influence was confined to seasonal sandalwood fleets and coastal Dominican missions [@PereiradosSa2026History; @Villiers1994Vanishing]. Regional population expanded slowly from 160k in 1515 to 210k in 1700, yielding an aggregate density of 1.241,36 persons per 100 km² (12,41 persons per km²). The population was heavily concentrated in the interior mountains of Ermera, Ainaro and Bobonaro, where traditional swidden agriculture provided subsistence insulated from coastal pirate raids and slave raiding [@Thomaz2020Cardoso]. The introduction of maize (*Zea mays*) in the mid-seventeenth century provided an energetic buffer against recurrent seasonal droughts, stimulating modest demographic growth [@Almeida2024Symbology].

### Topasse Ascendancy, Kingdom Rivalries and the Foundation of Dili (1700 to 1860)

Between 1700 and 1860, regional population grew from 210k to 340k (2.009,81 persons per 100 km²). This period witnessed intense political fragmentation as the Topasse warlords resisted direct crown administration from Lifau, eventually forcing Governor Telles de Meneses to relocate the colonial seat to Dili in 1769 [@Hagerdal2022Chapter; @ROQUE2012Marriage]. Dili grew slowly from a swampy military garrison into a permanent trading port, while interior kingdoms maintained autonomous tributary relations. The gradual spread of coffee planting in the early nineteenth century began to alter regional settlement patterns, encouraging the nucleation of trading hamlets along mule tracks connecting highland plantations to Dili and Liquica [@Kammen2025Colonial].

### Administrative Penetration, Pacification and Plantation Labour (1860 to 1927)

Following the reforms of Governor Afonso de Castro in the 1860s, the colonial state attempted to convert customary tribute into direct monetary taxation, prompting violent resistance that culminated in the Great Rebellion of Manufahi (1895 to 1912) [@Roque2016Unruly; @Bovensiepen2019Pacificati]. Despite widespread wartime destruction and epidemic outbreaks during pacification campaigns, population rose from 340k in 1860 to 380k in 1900 and 451k in 1927. The defeat of Dom Boaventura enabled the establishment of civil administrative posts throughout the interior, facilitating compulsory road building and expanding coffee acreage, which drew thousands of highland cultivators into seasonal wage labour networks [@Sousa2023Insurrect; @Sousa2023Chapter].

### The Pacific War, Japanese Occupation and Demographic Collapse (1927 to 1946)

Population expanded to 463k by 1936 before the catastrophe of World War II struck the island [@Duek2025Introduction]. The Japanese invasion of February 1942 and the subsequent three-year guerrilla campaign devastated the agrarian economy. Heavy requisitioning of rice and maize, forced labour details and scorched-earth reprisals by Japanese forces and armed irregulars devastated traditional food production [@Duek2025Introduction; @Rocha2020Tempos]. Famine and epidemic malaria devastated the central coffee valleys and southern plains. By 1946, regional population had collapsed to 420k, a net deficit of 43k persons compared to 1936 (and an estimated 60k deficit relative to pre-war projected growth), representing the most severe demographic catastrophe in modern Timorese history [@Fernandes2022Australias].

### Post-War Reconstruction, Public Health and Late Colonial Apex (1946 to 1975)

Following the restoration of Portuguese administration in 1945, the colonial government implemented metropolitan development plans (*Planos de Fomento*) focused on urban reconstruction, transport infrastructure and public health [@Madeira2010Manipulation; @Kammen2018Progress]. Systematic anti-malaria spraying and yaws eradication campaigns dramatically reduced child mortality, triggering rapid population recovery [@Saikia2011Investigation]. Population increased to 442k in 1950, 517k in 1960, 609k in 1970 and 660k in 1975. Dili expanded rapidly from a ruined settlement of 7k inhabitants in 1946 into an administrative and educational centre exceeding 25k residents by 1975, while secondary centres such as Baucau, Ermera, Maliana and Viqueque developed active municipal markets [@Philpott2007Another; @Silva2022Chapter; @Kubiak2021East].

The settlement hierarchy of Portuguese Timor exhibited a three-tiered structural organisation:
1. Primary colonial metropolises and administrative posts: Dili (represented by its core administrative posts Dom Aleixo, Vera Cruz, Cristo Rei and Nain Feto, aggregating over 60k residents across its suburban perimeter by 1975) served as the primary administrative, fiscal and educational capital [@Philpott2007Another; @Silva2022Chapter]. Secondary administrative capitals included Baucau (26,51k peak) commanding the eastern plateau and airport, Pante Makassar (20,89k peak) serving the Oecusse enclave and Manatuto (26,13k peak) bridging the north coast corridor [@Tosun2025Influence].
2. Regional agricultural and market centres: Viqueque (43,56k peak) commanding the southern fertile rice plains, Lautem (36,56k peak) managing the eastern karst frontier, Ainaro (35,38k peak) anchoring the southern slopes of Mount Ramelau, Hatulia (20,61k peak) and Ermera (20,24k peak) coordinating highland coffee processing and transport [@Kammen2025Colonial; @Almeida2025Baldios; @Sousa2023Chapter].
3. Secondary highland posts and coastal ports: Maubisse (12,45k peak), Letefoho (12,4k peak), Maubara (12,29k peak), Uato-Lari (10,6k peak) and Laga (10,29k peak), serving as local administrative seats, Catholic mission stations and market gathering points for dispersed rural sucos [@Bovensiepen2022Chapter; @Clamagirand1972Travail].

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis in Portuguese Timor faces several significant archival and methodological constraints:
1. Archival destruction during the Pacific War: the complete destruction of Dili during the Japanese invasion of 1942 and Allied aerial bombing incinerated the central government secretariat, municipal archives and civil registry offices, necessitating reliance on metropolitan duplicates preserved in Lisbon and post-war reconstruction estimates [@Duek2025Introduction; @Rocha2020Tempos].
2. Tax evasion and census undercounting in interior sucos: head taxes (*imposto de capitacao*) provided strong economic incentives for rural *liurais* and *chefes de suco* to under-report active adult populations and hide remote mountain hamlets from visiting census commissions [@Sousa2023Insurrect; @Kammen2017Metaphors].
3. Shifting administrative boundaries: colonial administrative posts (*postos administrativos*) and *sucos* were repeatedly re-demarcated during military pacification campaigns (1860 to 1912) and post-war administrative reorganisations, complicating longitudinal spatial tracking [@Roque2016Unruly; @Leach2015Politics].
4. Perishable domestic architecture: traditional Timorese domestic architecture was constructed from timber, bamboo and thatch (*uma lulik*), leaving minimal archaeological surface signatures compared to stone or baked-brick monuments, making field validation dependent on oral histories and colonial cartographic coordinates [@MeitznerYode2025Indigenous].

# Conclusion

Over four and a half centuries of Portuguese presence, the demographic history of Portuguese Timor evolved from an autonomous archipelago of sandalwood-producing kingdoms into an integrated colonial territory. Population grew from 160k in 1515 to an apex of 660k in 1975 across 16.917 km² of mountainous territory. This growth was interrupted by anti-colonial warfare and the devastation of the Pacific War (1942 to 1945), when Japanese military occupation and famine caused the loss of over 43k lives.

The resilience of the Timorese population was rooted in customary social structures and adaptable swidden agriculture. The sacred house (*uma lulik*) and lineage alliances enabled rural communities to absorb colonial fiscal shocks, resist military pacification and rebuild highland agriculture in the post-war era. The post-1945 expansion of public health services, transport infrastructure and educational networks laid the demographic foundation for the modern nation-state of Timor-Leste.
